The sandwich structures were developed for radar absorption and load-bearing capability.
The front face skin was glass fiber epoxy matrix composite with carbon black.
The back face skin was carbon fiber epoxy matrix composite.
The core was polyurethane foam reinforced with graphite powder or carbonyl iron.
Carbon black loading in the front face skin was varied from 6wt.% to 8wt.%.
Graphite powder loading in the foam core was varied from 5wt.% to 30wt.%.
Carbonyl iron loading in the foam core was varied from 30wt.% to 55wt.%.
Compression molding was used to prepare the face skins and sandwich structures.
The structures were characterized for a frequency range of 2–18 GHz.
The maximum attenuation observed was -31.85 dB.
The maximum attenuation was achieved with 6wt.% carbon black and 20wt.% graphite powder.
The optimal structure achieved 100% RCS reduction at nine different frequencies.
The average RCS reduction was 88% in X-band and 95% in Ku-band.
Graphite powder was more effective at higher frequencies (Ku-band).
Carbonyl iron was more effective at lower frequencies (X-band).
The ABC design had 10 different structures tested.
The ABABC design had 1 structure tested.
The ABABC design showed broader attenuation peaks.
The structures achieved almost zero radar signature at multiple frequencies.
The study demonstrated the ability to tune absorption by varying filler loading.
The structures are suitable for stealth aircraft and electromagnetic interference shielding.
The structures can be used in wind turbine blades to reduce radar interference.
The research was conducted at the Institute of Space Technology, Islamabad, Pakistan.
The raw materials were supplied by Advanced Engineering Research Organization (AERO), Pakistan.
The study was published in the Journal of Sandwich Structures and Materials.
